overview: This five-document file traces an exchange between the Flour Millers’ Export Association and the U.S. Department of State concerning postwar opportunities for West Coast mills to export flour to Japan and Korea. Martin F. Smith initially asks about Japanese milling capacity and export procedures, and Francis A. Linville replies that Japan may have capacity of 200,000 metric tons per month, compared with reported 1940 production of roughly 100,000 tons per month, while noting that U.S. grain and flour shipments are procured by the Department of Agriculture’s Production and Marketing Administration. Smith then proposes a private barter arrangement involving flour and Japanese products; the State Department advises consultation with the Department of the Army because such trade required approval through the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. An internal memorandum documents the revision of that reply into a somewhat more encouraging form.

subfiles.title: Smith inquiry about exporting flour to Japan and Korea
subfiles.from: Martin F. Smith, Flour Millers’ Export Association
subfiles.to: Francis A. Linville, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.about: Smith requests information on Japanese flour-milling capacity and how a West Coast mill might export flour to Japan or Korea, possibly through barter.
subfiles.summary: Smith recalls that West Coast millers exported flour to Japan and Korea during the early 1920s and explains that he has been unable to determine the postwar prospects for resuming that trade. An agent for a West Coast mill has requested quotations and apparently anticipates arranging a barter transaction. Smith asks Linville either to explain the appropriate procedure or to route the inquiry to the proper authorities.

subfiles.title: Linville reply on Japanese milling capacity and federal procurement
subfiles.from: Francis A. Linville, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.to: Martin F. Smith, Flour Millers’ Export Association
subfiles.about: Linville provides estimates of Japanese milling capacity and directs the miller to the Department of Agriculture for procurement information.
subfiles.summary: Linville reports that fragmentary information suggests Japan may possess flour-milling capacity of as much as 200,000 metric tons per month, while reported production in 1940 averaged approximately 100,000 metric tons monthly. He explains that all grain and flour exported to Japan and Korea is procured by the Department of Agriculture’s Production and Marketing Administration. The interested mill should therefore obtain procurement instructions from the Agriculture Department.

subfiles.title: Smith follow-up proposing a Tokyo barter arrangement
subfiles.from: Martin F. Smith, Flour Millers’ Export Association
subfiles.to: Francis A. Linville, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.about: Smith asks how a West Coast miller could exchange flour for Japanese products through an agent in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Smith thanks Linville for the September 24 response but says that the West Coast miller has renewed his request for guidance. The miller wants to ship flour to Japan through an agent in Tokyo and receive Japanese products in return. Smith acknowledges that the Production and Marketing Administration is already supplying Japan with flour but asks whether a private barter arrangement is nevertheless possible.

subfiles.title: Linville reply referring barter proposal to the Department of the Army
subfiles.from: Francis A. Linville, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.to: Martin F. Smith, Flour Millers’ Export Association
subfiles.about: Linville advises that the proposed barter transaction might be possible but would have to be pursued through the occupation authorities.
subfiles.summary: Linville characterizes the proposed transaction as unusual but potentially workable. Because such arrangements had to be made through the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, he recommends that Smith discuss the plan with Colonel O. J. Baldwin of the Department of the Army’s Civil Affairs Division. Baldwin could then approach the occupation authorities if he considered the proposal feasible.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers

subfiles.title: Whitman memorandum suggesting a less-negative barter reply
subfiles.to: Francis A. Linville, International Resources Division
subfiles.about: Whitman recommends revising the draft response to Smith so that it presents the barter proposal as potentially feasible and directs him to the Army.
subfiles.summary: Whitman judges the attached draft reply to be more negative than necessary and proposes replacement language. The suggested paragraph says the unusual arrangement might possibly be worked out, while emphasizing that it must proceed through the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. It recommends consultation with Colonel Baldwin, who could communicate with the occupation authorities if he found the plan feasible; this language substantially anticipates the reply on page 4.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers

interest: The file offers a compact view of how private American firms sought access to the Japanese market during the occupation and how civilian trade initiatives were constrained by federal procurement and SCAP authority. Its quantitative estimate of Japanese milling capacity is useful evidence about contemporary U.S. assessments of industrial recovery. The October 8 memorandum is especially revealing because it preserves the bureaucratic editing behind the official response, showing an effort to adopt a less discouraging tone while still channeling the proposal through military occupation authorities.
